entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen10302" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Cry Sent Forth from the Prison to the Best of Friends</title> <div sID="gen10303" type="x-p"/> This the last of the eight Davidic Psalms, which are derived by their inscriptions from the time of the persecution by Saul (vid., on Ps 34), is inscribed: <hi type="italic">A Meditation by David, when he was in the cave, a Prayer</hi>. Of these eight Psalms, <reference osisRef="Ps.52.1-Ps.52.9">Psa 52:1-9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.54.1-Ps.54.7">Psa 54:1-7</reference> also bear the name of <hi type="italic">Maskı̂l</hi> (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1-Ps.32.11">Psa 32:1-11</reference>); and in this instance תּפּלּה (which occurs besides as an inscription only in <reference osisRef="Ps.90.1">Psa 90:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.1">Psa 102:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.3.1">Psa 3:1</reference>) is further added, which looks like an explanation of the word <hi type="italic">maskı̂l</hi> (not in use out of the range of Psalm-poetry). The article of במערה, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.57.1">Psa 57:1</reference>, points to the cave of Adullam (1 Sam. 22) or the cave of Engedi (1 Sam. 24), which latter, starting from a narrow concealed entrance, forms such a labyrinthine maze of passages and vaults that the torches and lines of explorers have not to the present time been able to reach the extremities of it. <div eID="gen10303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10304" type="x-p"/> The Psalm does not contain any sure signs of a post-Davidic age; still it appears throughout to be an imitation of older models, and pre-eminently by means of Psa 142:2. (cf. Psa 77:2.) and <reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.77.4">Psa 77:4</reference>) it comes into a relation of dependence to Ps 77, which is also noticeable in <reference osisRef="Ps.143.1-Ps.143.12">Psa 143:1-12</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.142.5">Psa 142:5</reference> with Psa 77:12.). The referring back of the two Psalms to David comes under one and the same judgment.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.142.1-Ps.142.3">Psa 142:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen10304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10305" type="x-p"/> The emphasis of the first two lines rests upon אל־ה. Forsaken by all created beings, he confides in Jahve. He turns to Him in pathetic and importunate prayer (זעק, the parallel word being התחנּן, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.30.9">Psa 30:9</reference>), and that not merely inwardly (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.15">Exo 14:15</reference>), but with his voice (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.3.5">Psa 3:5</reference>) - for audible prayer reacts soothingly, strengtheningly, and sanctifyingly upon the praying one - he pours out before Him his trouble which distracts his thoughts (שׁפך שׂיח as in <reference osisRef="Ps.102.1">Psa 102:1</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.62.9">Psa 62:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.64.2">Psa 64:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.16">1Sa 1:16</reference>), he lays open before Him everything that burdens and distresses him. Not as though He did not also know it without all this; on the contrary, when his spirit (רוּחי as in <reference osisRef="Ps.143.4">Psa 143:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.77.4">Psa 77:4</reference>, cf. נפשׁי <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.7">Jon 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.5">Psa 107:5</reference>, לבּי <reference osisRef="Ps.61.3">Psa 61:3</reference>) within him (עלי, see <reference osisRef="Ps.42.5">Psa 42:5</reference>) is enshrouded and languishes, just this is his consolation, that Jahve is intimately acquainted with his way together with the dangers that threaten him at every step, and therefore also understands how to estimate the title (right) and meaning of his complaints. The <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> of ואתּה is the same as in 1Ki 8:36, cf. Ps 35. Instead of saying: then I comfort myself with the fact that, etc., he at once declares the fact with which he comforts himself. Supposing this to be the case, there is no need for any alteration of the text in order to get over that which is apparently incongruous in the relation of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference></hi> to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference></hi>.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.142.6-Ps.142.7">Psa 142:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen10306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10307" type="x-p"/> His request now ascends all the more confident of being answered, and becomes calm, being well-grounded in his feebleness and the superiority of his enemies, and aiming at the glorifying of the divine Name. In <reference osisRef="Ps.142.7">Psa 142:7</reference> רנּתי calls to mind <reference osisRef="Ps.17.1">Psa 17:1</reference>; the first confirmation, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.8">Psa 79:8</reference>, and the second, Psa 18:18. But this is the only passage in the whole Psalter where the poet designates the “distress” in which he finds himself as a prison (מסגּר). V. 8 <hi type="italic">b</hi> brings the whole congregation of the righteous in in the praising of the divine Name. The poet therefore does not after all find himself so absolutely alone, as it might seem according to Psa 142:5. He is far from regarding himself as the only righteous person. He is only a member of a community or church whose destiny is interwoven with his own, and which will glory in his deliverance as its own; for “if one member is honoured, all the members rejoice with it” (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.26">1Co 12:26</reference>). We understand the differently interpreted יכתּירוּ after this “rejoicing with” (συγχαίρει). The lxx, Syriac, and Aquilaz render: the righteous wait for me; but to wait is כּתּר and not הכתּיר. The modern versions, on the other hand, almost universally, like Luther after Felix Pratensis, render: the righteous shall surround me (flock about me), in connection with which, as Hengstenberg observes, בּי denotes the tender sympathy they fell with him: crowding closely upon me. But there is no instance of a verb of surrounding (אפף, סבב, סבב, עוּד, עטר, הקּיף) taking בּ; the accusative stands with הכתּיר in <reference osisRef="Hab.1.4">Hab 1:4</reference>, and כּתּר in <reference osisRef="Ps.22.13">Psa 22:13</reference>, in the signification <hi type="italic">cingere</hi>. Symmachus (although erroneously rendering: τὸ ὄνομά σου στεφανώσονται δίκαιοι), Jerome (<hi type="italic">in me coronabuntur justi</hi>), Parchon, Aben-Ezra, Coccejus, and others, rightly take יכתּירוּ as a denominative from כּתר, to put on a crown or to crown (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.14.18">Pro 14:18</reference>): on account of me the righteous shall adorn themselves as with crowns, i.e., shall triumph, that Thou dealest bountifully with me (an echo of <reference osisRef="Ps.13.6">Psa 13:6</reference>). According to passages like Ps 64:11; <reference osisRef="Ps.40.17">Psa 40:17</reference>, one might have expected בּו instead of בּי. But the close of Ps 22 (Psa 22:23.), cf. Psa 140:12., shows that בי is also admissible. The very fact that David contemplates his own destiny and the destiny of his foes in a not merely ideal but foreordainedly causal connection with the general end of the two powers that stand opposed to one another in the world, belongs to the characteristic impress of the Psalms of David that come from the time of Saul’s persecution.  <chapter eID="Ps.142"/> <div eID="gen10307" type="x-p"/>
